strengths: The paper addresses a timely topic (learnable activations, revitalized by KANs) and provides a principled variance-preserving initialization for activations expressed in orthonormal bases, with clean closed-form second-moment results for Hermite and Fourier activations that unify forward and backward gains (extending He et al., 2015).

Evaluation goes beyond the small-scale (MNIST-style) experiments that the authors themselves criticize in the literature: experiments are run on ImageNet-1k with ConvNeXt-T and on GPT-2 (124M) with OpenWebText, which lends credibility to the empirical claims.

Useful ablations are provided: degree of the activation, initialization scheme (fitted vs. theory-based), learnability of coefficients, and clamping; the code and training setup are described in enough detail (and released) to support reproducibility.

Practical engineering contributions (custom CUDA kernels, stable computation via log-gamma, recurrence formulations) and honest discussion of computational complexity (O(d^2) for explicit Hermite vs O(d) for recurrence) and of numerical pitfalls (aliasing in Fourier interpolation, Lipschitz behavior of derivatives).
weaknesses: The empirical gains over the static-activation baseline are marginal and inconsistent: on ImageNet-1k, Hermite improves top-1 by only ~0.3% (82.34 vs 82.04) and Fourier actually underperforms GELU on validation (81.91 vs 82.04) despite better training loss (2.775 vs 2.819), suggesting overfitting rather than genuinely better generalization; GPT-2 perplexity differences (18.39 vs 19.24) are modest. No statistical significance tests, error bars, or multi-seed variance are reported, so the central claim of 'significant improvements' is not fully supported.

Novelty is limited: learnable polynomial/orthogonal activations have been explored before (e.g., Hermite polynomial activations of Lokhande et al. 2020, polynomial activations of Chrysos et al., Chebyshev/Hermite activations of Nebioglu & Iliev), and the initialization theory is a fairly direct application of the He et al. variance-preserving framework to orthonormal bases; the polynomial-mapping proposition (3.32) is essentially trivial and well known.

No comparison against other learnable-activation baselines (e.g., Pade activations, spline/KAN-style activations, wavelet activations, adaptable activation networks), which is necessary to position the contribution within the very literature the paper surveys.

The variance-preservation analysis assumes the pre-activation input remains Gaussian (Hermite) or uniform (Fourier) with mean zero throughout, but with learnable activation coefficients and deep composition the input distribution shifts during training; the paper does not empirically validate that the gain-equality property holds beyond initialization, weakening the causal story for the observed stability.

The tropical activation component is underdeveloped: no second-moment/gain analysis is provided ('deferred to later work'), the initialization is ad hoc ('all ones... empirically'), and its theoretical motivation (tropical rational maps) is not connected to any measured benefit; it performs comparably to, not better than, Hermite while adding a separate line of complexity.

The theoretical framework covers only initialization; there is no analysis of training dynamics of the learnable coefficients (e.g., whether they drift away from variance-preserving configurations, interactions with weight decay—which is only handled heuristically by excluding activation coefficients).

Memory/compute overhead is acknowledged as significant for the explicit formulation, but no wall-clock training time or throughput numbers are reported, making the cost-benefit trade-off hard to assess.

Some writing/presentation issues reduce polish (e.g., 'monominator' typo, Figure 6 caption inconsistencies, unusual polemical tone in the KAN digression and extended related work), and several important details (number of seeds, hyperparameter search for degrees) are only partially specified.

strengths: The paper is commendable in attempting to scale learnable activation functions beyond toy settings: experiments on ConvNeXt-T with ImageNet-1k and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText are far more substantial than the small-scale (MNIST-level) evaluations common in this literature.

The closed-form second-moment derivations for orthonormal bases (Hermite, Fourier) are correct and cleanly presented, and connecting the choice of basis to the assumed input distribution is a sensible organizing principle.
Ablation studies (degree, initialization, learnability, clamping) are provided, and the paper is transparent that fixed configurations/seeds were used for comparability.
Engineering contributions (dedicated CUDA kernels, stable evaluation via log-gamma and recurrences, complexity analysis) and stated code release aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are marginal and likely within noise: e.g., 82.34 vs 82.04 top-1 on ImageNet-1k and 18.39 vs 18.72 validation PPL on OpenWebText, each from a single run with a fixed seed. No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported, so the central claim of 'significantly improving' over GELU is not adequately supported.

The theoretical analysis rests on idealized assumptions (i.i.d. inputs following N(0,1) or uniform distributions, zero-mean weights, independence between x and W) that do not hold in deep networks in practice; the paper provides no empirical verification that variance (forward or backward) is actually preserved during training in the tested architectures.

The gain-equality conditions yield only one constraint (Eq. 14/26) on many coefficients; the resulting initializations (e.g., a_k = 1/k^p with a chosen p) are largely heuristic, and the tropical activation — a headline contribution — has no variance-preserving theory at all (coefficients are simply set to 1), making its inclusion feel disconnected from the paper's core technical narrative.

Novelty is limited: learnable polynomial, trigonometric, and rational activations have been extensively studied (the related work itself catalogues dozens of predecessors), and the observation that deep polynomially-activated networks are polynomial mappings (Prop. 3.32) is a straightforward induction on a well-known fact.

The practical value of the proposed activations over the baseline is questionable given the added computational cost (O(d^2) FLOPs/memory for the explicit Hermite form), which is only briefly acknowledged; no throughput/training-time comparison is reported.

Several issues are deferred to future work without justification, e.g., the second-order moment for tropical activations, and the interesting rational tropical extension (Appendix F) is never evaluated on actual tasks.

Presentation problems: Figure 7 is illegible (overlapping curves, cut-off legend), the paper oscillates between framing the contribution as theory, library, or empirical study, and the lengthy KAN digression (Appendix I) is editorializing rather than substantive.

strengths: Rigorous and clean variance-preserving initialization theory for activations expressed in orthonormal bases (Hermite, Fourier), yielding closed-form second-moment expressions and a scalable coefficient initialization (Theorem 3.15) that provably equalizes forward and backward gains in the limit — a genuine technical contribution beyond the 'fit a classic activation' trick of prior work.

Experiments at a scale rarely seen in the learnable-activation literature: ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText, rather than the typical small-scale (MNIST/CIFAR) evaluations the paper itself correctly criticizes.

Useful ablations covering degree, initialization scheme, learnability, and clamping (Tables 3–6), which support the paper's claims that the proposed initialization matters and that learnability (rather than the basis family alone) drives the gains.

Careful engineering discussion: numerical stability of Hermite evaluation (log-gamma formulation, dedicated CUDA kernels, recurrence for O(d) complexity), float16 concerns, aliasing in Fourier interpolation, and weight-decay exclusion for activation coefficients.
Honest and substantive related-work section, including a well-informed critical dissection of KANs and the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem, which correctly situates this line of work.
Code and model weights released, and fixed hyperparameters/seeds across configurations for comparability.
weaknesses: Limited headline novelty: learnable polynomial/trigonometric activations are well explored (Lokhande et al. 2020, Zhou et al. 2019, Chrysos et al., Padé-based activations, KAN follow-ups). The genuinely new elements are the initialization scheme and the tropical activation; Proposition 3.32 (deep polynomial networks are polynomial mappings) is a textbook induction result, and the tropical activation is used without the variance analysis the paper is built around (the generalized extreme-value moment is explicitly deferred to future work), making its 'all ones' initialization ad hoc.

Empirical gains are modest and reported as 'extremal values' over trials with an unclear number of seeds, without statistical significance testing. ImageNet top-1 improvements over the GELU baseline are ~0.1–0.3% (82.04 → 82.34); GPT-2 perplexity improves from 19.24 to 18.39, which is more convincing but still small for a 124M model trained once per configuration.

No comparison against any prior learnable-activation baseline (e.g., Hermite polynomial activations of Lokhande et al., Padé activations, Chebyshev, KAN-style splines) on the large-scale tasks, despite an extensive related-work section — the only comparisons are static GELU/ReLU and the paper's own variants. This makes it impossible to judge whether the specific proposed families matter versus learnable activations in general.

The theory–practice gap is not empirically validated: the variance analysis assumes N(0,1) (or uniform) inputs and E[W]=0 independence, but the paper never measures actual per-layer signal/gradient variances during training to confirm the initialization behaves as predicted in real architectures (LayerNorm-heavy models like ConvNeXt/GPT-2 complicate the assumptions).

Configurations are selected inconsistently (Hermite degree 3, Fourier/Tropical degree 6; Hermite initialized from Thm 3.15, Fourier/Tropical from GELU/ones), and the best configuration per family appears to be picked from the same evaluation data, raising mild selection-bias concerns. Notably, Fourier initialized from GELU has better training loss but worse validation accuracy than GELU, and this overfitting pattern is not analyzed.

Several presentation issues: Figure 2's caption/claim is confusingly worded (it shows degree 3 fits GELU poorly), 'Newtone methods' typo, Table 1 mixes different degrees/initializations without explanation, and the discussion of Lipschitz continuity for Hermite activations (Remark 3.12) is left as a hand-wave ('keep the Lipschitz constant under control') with no mechanism.

Scope is narrow: one vision model and one language model, each trained once per configuration, with no results on other architectures (e.g., ResNet, ViT at other scales) or downstream tasks, so the generality of the claims ('significantly improve over GPT-2 and ConvNeXt') rests on two settings.

strengths: The paper makes a coherent contribution unifying variance-preserving initialization with orthonormal bases (Hermite, Fourier) and tropical polynomials, deriving closed-form forward/backward gains (Theorems 3.8, 3.13, 3.19) with complete proofs in the appendix.

Rare and convincing large-scale empirical validation for learnable activations: ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet1k and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText, both with 3 seeds, mean ± std reporting, and stated no-cherry-picking protocol. Hermite and Tropical activations match or slightly exceed GELU baselines.

Thorough ablation studies covering degree, initialization scheme, learnability, and clamping, which substantiate each design claim (e.g., learnable coefficients and the proposed init are clearly necessary).

Attention to practicality: explicit parallel Hermite formulas, dedicated CUDA forward/backward kernels (Algs. 1-6), O(d) recurrence, floating-point considerations, and Hermite-interpolation-based fitting of classical activations for fine-tuning, plus a stated release in a library.

The observation that orthogonal bases yield closed-form second moments is a clean, useful idea that directly addresses a real weakness of prior learnable activations (e.g., rational activations requiring fitting tricks).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: learnable Hermite activations (Turian et al. 2009; Lokhande et al. 2020), Fourier/periodic activations (SIREN, DCT-based ENN), and tropical views of ReLU networks (Zhang et al. 2018; Smyrnis & Maragos 2019) all exist; the main new element is the initialization analysis. The claim of 'first time such activations can lead to improvements at scale' is overstated given prior polynomial-activation works.

The theoretical result in Appendix F (polynomially activated networks are polynomial mappings of degree at most d^L) is elementary and well known; presenting it as a headline contribution inflates the paper's perceived depth.

The variance analysis relies on strong and unrealistic assumptions: pre-activations are assumed N(0,1) or U(-pi,pi) and independent across coordinates, which does not hold in trained deep networks; there is no empirical measurement of actual activation/gradient variance during training to validate the theory's practical relevance.

Improvements are marginal and statistically fragile: on ImageNet, Hermite gains +0.17 Top-1 over GELU with seed std of ±0.13, and Fourier underperforms GELU; GPT-2 validation loss gains (~0.02) are small despite consistency. The paper would be more convincing with significance tests or more seeds.

No comparison against competing learnable activation baselines (Padé/Safe-Padé, KAN-style activations, Chebyshev, SPLASH) despite an extended related-work section discussing them; the ablations only compare against the static GELU baseline.

Practical cost is significant: 30-90% slower training than baseline, which weakens the claimed relevance for 'improving efficiency of large-scale learning'; the promised kernel optimizations remain future work.

Writing issues: the abstract's library name is missing/truncated, FLOPs/Act. column in Table 1 is confusing, some proofs (Prop. C.8/C.9) have sloppy intermediate steps, and the tropical activation's gain result (Thm 3.19) only holds in an n→∞ limit while experiments use degree 6.

The Hermite and Fourier activations are analyzed under different input distributions (Gaussian vs. uniform) without justification of which applies in real networks, and Remark 3.15's alternative scalings are explored only anecdotally.

strengths: Unusually thorough large-scale empirical validation for an activation-function paper: ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k, GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText, CIFAR-10 fine-tuning, with 3 seeds, reported mean ± standard error, and ablations over degree, initialization, learnability, and clamping (Tables 3–6).

The variance-preserving initialization derived via orthonormal bases (Hermite, Fourier) yields clean closed-form second-moment/gain expressions (Thms 3.8, 3.13), and the paper is honest about distribution-matching assumptions (Gaussian for Hermite, uniform for Fourier).

Implementation details are concrete: parallel Hermite formulas, CUDA kernels for forward/backward passes, amplitude-phase Fourier formulation, FLOP/parameter accounting, and a candid limitations section acknowledging 30–90% training slowdown.
The extended related work and the digression on KANs provide useful context on why prior polynomial-activation evaluations were inconclusive.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: learnable Hermite, Fourier, and polynomial activations have been studied extensively before (Lokhande et al. 2020, Sitzmann et al. 2020, Padé-activation works, KAN-adjacent literature, all acknowledged by the authors). The main new element is applying the standard He et al. forward/backward gain analysis to these known function families, which is a fairly incremental technical contribution; the Appendix F proof that polynomial networks are polynomial mappings is trivial.

The headline empirical claims are overclaimed relative to the evidence. On ImageNet-1k the Hermite gain is +0.17% Top-1 (within ~1 SE of GELU) and Fourier actually underperforms GELU (81.82 vs 82.01); on GPT-2 the perplexity gap is ~0.1–0.4 PPL. Claims such as 'show for the first time that such activations can lead to improvements over traditional static functions' are not supported by statistically meaningful margins.

The tropical activation analysis is largely degenerate: with the proposed initialization, the n→∞ limit is exactly a scaled ReLU (Appendix E), so the 'novel' tropical activation reduces at initialization to the baseline it is compared against, undermining its conceptual contribution.

The theoretical framework rests on questionable assumptions: pre-activations are assumed independent, identically distributed as N(0,1) or U(−π,π), which is unrealistic during training of deep networks (and after the very first weight updates), and the inputs x_i are assumed independent and uniformly distributed (Sec. 3.1), contradicting the later mean-0/variance-1 assumption (Asm. 3.4). No empirical verification of the moment assumptions is provided.

The claim of training 'without additional clamping mechanisms' is contradicted by the paper itself: Table 6 ablates clamping, weight decay is explicitly excluded from activation coefficients, and gradient clipping (5.0) appears in the CIFAR configuration.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers suggest weak experimental bookkeeping: e.g., Table 1 reports Fourier deg-6 at 81.82% Top-1 with the proposed initialization, while ablation Table 4 reports the same configuration ('Fourier, deg 6, Thrm 3.13') at 80.93%; Hermite deg-3 appears as 82.34% in Tables 3–6 but 82.18% in Table 1. No explanation is given.

Missing comparisons against other learnable-activation baselines (Safe-Padé, SIREN, Chebyshev/KAN-style activations) at matched budget; thus it is unclear whether gains come from the specific basis/initialization or simply from added learnable parameters. Also, the fine-tuning experiment (Sec 4.5/O) compares against a GELU baseline whose activation cannot adapt at all, making the 'clear superiority' unsurprising.

Reproducibility and presentation issues: the abstract ends with 'available in the library' without naming the library, and no code release is stated; several notation/citation formatting errors ('Newtone', 'Welscher' vs. Berrut & Trefethen-style references) and unexplained footnotes (e.g., the bare '2' after Eq. discussion on p.8) further weaken the manuscript.

strengths: The variance-preserving initialization derived for orthonormal function bases (Hermite, Fourier) and the tropical activation is elegant, well-motivated by the closed-form second-order moments, and correctly extends the classical He-initiation analysis to learnable activations.

Rare large-scale empirical validation for activation-function research: ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k and GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText, with 3 seeds, fixed hyperparameters, and mean±std reporting — most prior work on learnable activations only used small datasets like MNIST, which the paper itself correctly criticizes.
Useful ablations covering the degree, the initialization scheme, learnability of coefficients, and clamping (Tables 3-6), which substantiate the individual design choices.

Practical engineering contributions: explicit parallelizable Hermite formula, recurrence-based CUDA kernels, FLOP/memory analysis, and weight-decay considerations for learnable coefficients; a library is provided, supporting reproducibility.
Extensive and scholarly related work (Appendices J-K), including a lucid critique of the KAN/Kolmogorov-Arnold positioning that is a service to the community.

The paper addresses the real issue of exploding activations/gradients for polynomial activations without auxiliary stabilization mechanisms (no SoftSign, ReLU-mixing, or normalization), which is a genuine step beyond prior polynomial-activation works.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are modest and of questionable statistical significance: on ImageNet-1k, Hermite's Top-1 improvement over GELU is ~0.17% with error bars (82.18±0.13 vs 82.01±0.04) that do not cleanly separate; Fourier actually underperforms GELU on ImageNet; the GPT-2 validation loss improvement is ~0.024 nats — small even if consistent. The abstract and discussion overstate these results.

Missing comparison against competing learnable-activation baselines (KAN, Padé/Safe-Padé, spline activations, Zhuo et al. 2024 polynomial composition activations) on the large-scale tasks, so it is unclear whether the proposed method is actually the best learnable-activation approach or just a viable one.

The theoretical claim that polynomially activated networks are multivariate polynomial mappings (Appendix F, Prop F.3) is a straightforward induction that will be obvious to most readers; presenting it as a headline contribution inflates the perceived novelty.

Hermite and Fourier activations have been studied before (Lokhande et al. 2020, Nebioglu & Iliev 2023, Zhuo et al. 2024, Sitzmann et al. 2020 for periodic activations); the incremental novelty is mainly the closed-form gain computation via orthogonality and applying it at scale.

The tropical activation's variance-preserving initialization holds only in the n→∞ limit and effectively reduces to a scaled ReLU; on vision it shows no consistent gain over GELU, weakening the case for including it as a core contribution.
Training is 30-90% slower than baselines, which limits practical impact given the marginal accuracy/loss gains; inference-time benefit claims are not quantified with wall-clock numbers.

Presentation issues: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('available in the library.' — the library name is missing), some references are incomplete (e.g., Karpathy 2022), and the assumption that layer inputs are N(0,1) or uniform is only approximately satisfied in trained networks, with no analysis of initialization robustness to distribution shift during training.
